paragraphs: Friend, this passage is heavy, and I'm not going to dress it up. Dinah was wronged, and the text says it plainly: Shechem "took her and lay with her by force" (Genesis 34:2). Her brothers were "filled with grief and fury" because it was "a thing that should not be done" (Genesis 34:7). So hear this first: the Bible does not shrug at what was done to her, and neither do I.

But watch what the fury does. The brothers answer "deceitfully," Simeon and Levi take their swords to a whole city of men who are still in pain, and the rest of the brothers loot everything (Genesis 34:13, 25, 27). A real wrong hurt Dinah, and the brothers' answer made a second wrong, a much bigger one. Their anger started in the right place and then went somewhere it never should have gone. I've seen a lot of dough rise in my day, and anger rises the same way if you leave it alone in a warm spot.

Look at what the passage doesn't do. Jacob says they've made him "a stench" and fears his household will be destroyed (Genesis 34:30). The brothers answer with a question, "Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?" (Genesis 34:31), and the chapter ends right there with no one explaining it away. Here's what I take from it, baker: being hurt is real, and feeling anger over a real wrong is not the problem. But what we do with that anger can leave us with a bigger mess than the one that started it, so we bring it to God before we pick up a sword. And Jacob's story isn't over yet.
